nodes.label: TETRIS3D
nodes.description: TETRIS3D is a 3D scene generation framework introduced in the paper "TETRIS3D: 3D SCENE GENERATION WITH OBJECTS THAT FIT TOGETHER." Built on TRELLIS.2, it is a generative framework for object-centric 3D scene reconstruction from a single image. The method sequentially generates objects autoregressively, explicitly conditioning each object on neighboring geometry and physical relations to achieve geometric and physical coherence among objects, even under occlusion. It reconstructs scenes in a topological order determined by VLM-inferred physical relations and dependencies using a two-stage pipeline consisting of sparse structure and structured latent generation. The framework includes visible-to-invisible attention layers, with sparse structure and structured latent generation models containing approximately 1.83B and 1.68B parameters respectively. TETRIS3D recovers objects which are physically and geometrically coherent as a scene, ensuring objects fit together through explicit conditioning on spatial context and physical relations between objects.

nodes.label: COMOB
nodes.description: COMOB is a large-scale, simulation-based dataset designed to provide physically consistent scenes with explicit object interaction annotations. It features 1.2 million scenes showcasing diverse object categories in physically stable configurations. The dataset includes per-object meshes, target-object images, normal maps, training viewpoints, and pairwise physical relation annotations. Additionally, it captures interaction-induced occlusions across various interaction types. Described in Section 3.4, COMOB is used for training and serves as a comprehensive resource for studying physical interactions in composite object scenes.

By conditioning on OBJECT INTERACTIONS, TETRIS3D ensures that object placements reflect meaningful spatial relationships and appropriate interaction types, resulting in coherent and contextually consistent 3D environments.

nodes.label: STRUCTURED LATENT GENERATION
nodes.description:
**Structured Latent Generation**

Structured Latent Generation represents a generation-stage model trained through a progressive curriculum of stages. This architecture is specifically designed for the generation phase, utilizing latent space structures to organize and facilitate the creation process. The training methodology employs a staged approach, moving through sequential curriculum steps to build complexity and capability. By focusing on the generation stage within a structured latent framework, the model achieves organized and coherent output generation. This methodology allows for systematic skill development, starting from foundational concepts and progressing toward more sophisticated generation tasks. The curriculum-based training ensures that the model develops a robust understanding of latent representations, enabling more controlled and effective generation capabilities across various domains.

nodes.label: CD-S
nodes.description: CD-S is a reconstruction quality metric, specifically a scene-level Chamfer Distance for surface reconstruction quality. It measures the Chamfer distance at the scene level by concatenating the point sets of all objects within a scene. This metric is used to evaluate reconstruction quality, with lower values indicating better performance, as denoted by CD-S ↓. It is referenced as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5.

nodes.label: CD-O
nodes.description: CD-O is a reconstruction quality metric that measures object-level Chamfer distance. It evaluates the geometric fidelity of individual object reconstructions by computing the Chamfer distance at the object level. CD-O is reported as a reconstruction quality metric in Table 1 and Table 5, with lower values indicating better performance (CD-O ↓). It is also referred to as Chamfer Distance for O, Chamfer Distance for Object reconstruction quality metric, Chamfer Distance for Objects metric, Chamfer distance for objects, and object-level Chamfer distance.

nodes.label: F1-S
nodes.description: F1-S is a reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate surface reconstruction performance at the scene level. It is an F1 score for S, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This scene-level F1 score serves as a key indicator of reconstruction quality and is reported as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-S ↑.

nodes.label: F1-O
nodes.description: F1-O is an object-level reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate the accuracy of reconstructed objects. It is an F1 score specifically for object reconstruction quality, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This metric appears in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-O ↑, indicating that higher values represent better reconstruction quality.

nodes.label: IOU-B
nodes.description:
**Intersection over Union for Bounding Box Reconstruction Quality (IoU-B)**

IoU-B is a reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate the accuracy of bounding box reconstruction. It is calculated as the Intersection over Union for bounding boxes, measuring the overlap between predicted and ground-truth boxes. This metric is commonly referenced in academic literature, specifically appearing in Table 1 and Table 5. It serves as a scene-level quality assessment tool, where higher values indicate better reconstruction quality. The metric is specifically designated as "IoU-B" and is used to quantify the performance of bounding box reconstruction methods.

nodes.label: ICP-ROT
nodes.description: ICP-ROT is a reconstruction quality metric used to measure rotation error in 3D reconstruction processes. It is specifically designed to quantify the rotation component of the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm's performance. This metric is typically evaluated at the scene level and reported in tables such as Table 1 and Table 5, where lower values indicate better reconstruction quality.

nodes.label: MMD
nodes.description:
**MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)**

MMD is a statistical metric used to measure the generative quality of models by comparing the distribution of generated data against the ground-truth object distribution. Reported in units of 10⁻³, it serves as a critical quality metric across multiple tables (Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5) within the research. A lower MMD value indicates a closer match between the generated and real data distributions, making it an effective measure of generative performance. This metric is formally defined in equation 14 and is also referenced as the Minimum Matching Distance.

nodes.label: COV
nodes.description: COV is a generation quality metric used to evaluate generative models against ground-truth object distributions. It measures coverage by calculating the fraction of ground-truth objects that are selected as the nearest neighbor of at least one generated object, with higher values indicating better performance (COV ↑). COV is defined in equation 14 and is reported as a metric in Table 1, Table 4, Tab. 4, and Table 5. It serves as both a coverage metric and a coverage generation quality metric, assessing how well generated objects cover the ground-truth distribution.

nodes.label: P-FID
nodes.description: P-FID, or Perceptual Fréchet Inception Distance, is a generation quality metric used to measure generative quality. It calculates the Fréchet distance between the distributions of generated and ground-truth objects in the feature space of the point-cloud feature extractor released with Point-E. As a lower score indicates better performance, it is often denoted as P-FID ↓. This metric is reported in various tables, including Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5, to evaluate the quality of generated point clouds.

nodes.label: UNI3D
nodes.description: UNI3D is a generation quality metric used to evaluate the semantic alignment between an input image and a generated point cloud. It is reported as a performance score where higher values indicate better quality, denoted as Uni3D ↑. This metric appears in Table 1 and Table 5 of the source material, where SAM-3D obtains a higher score. It serves as a key measure for assessing the fidelity and relevance of 3D point cloud generation relative to visual input.

nodes.label: ULIP
nodes.description: ULIP is a generation quality metric used to evaluate the semantic alignment between an input image and a generated point cloud. It is reported as a score where higher values indicate better performance, denoted as ULIP ↑. This metric appears in Table 1 and Table 5 of the source material, where SAM-3D obtains a higher score compared to other methods. As a semantic measure, ULIP assesses the quality of 3D generation by quantifying how well the generated point cloud corresponds to the input image.

nodes.label: PD
nodes.description: PD, or Penetration Depth, is a physical stability metric used to quantify the extent of penetration or overlap between entities, calculated using the formula PD = 1/N ∑ᵢ₌₁ᴺ ∑ⱼ max{0, -ϕⱼ(xᵢ)}. This metric is referenced in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where lower values (PD ↓) indicate better physical stability. While one description refers to it as a physical distance metric, the consistent context across all entries identifies PD as a physical stability metric focused on penetration depth.

nodes.label: DMEAN
nodes.description: DMEAN is a physical stability metric, also known as the Mean Distance metric, Mean Distance physical stability metric, Mean depth metric, Mean displacement metric, or Mean distance metric. It is a quantitative measure used to assess physical stability, with lower values indicating greater stability (Dmean ↓). DMEAN is documented as a metric in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5.

nodes.label: EPEAK
nodes.description: EPEAK is a physical stability metric, also referred to as the Peak Energy metric or Peak error metric. It is included in Table 1 and measured in Table 5. The metric follows a downward trend, where lower EPEAK values indicate better physical stability (↓ Epeak ↓).

nodes.label: OPEN BINS
nodes.description: OPEN BINS is a containment object type and a parametric primitive type. As a containment object type, OPEN BINS refers to a category of objects designed to hold or enclose other items, typically characterized by an open structure that allows for easy access and visibility of contents. As a parametric primitive type, OPEN BINS represents a fundamental geometric or data structure whose properties—such as dimensions, capacity, or shape—can be defined and adjusted through parameters. This dual classification indicates that OPEN BINS functions both as a practical container for physical or digital items and as a configurable primitive element within a modeling or design system. The open nature of the bins suggests they are intended for applications requiring frequent insertion, removal, or inspection of contained objects, while their parametric nature allows for customization to meet specific spatial or functional requirements.

Simultaneously, as a parametric primitive type, they serve as fundamental geometric building blocks defined by adjustable parameters, allowing for variations in shape, size, and configuration. This dual classification indicates that POLYGONAL BINS combine the functional purpose of containment with the technical characteristics of parameterized geometric primitives.

edges.description: TETRIS3D is a model trained on the ComOb dataset, a large-scale simulation-based composited object scene dataset introduced in the associated paper. Training Tetris3D requires scenes that capture diverse object interactions with physical relation annotations, which ComOb provides. Additionally, Tetris3D uses the ComOb generator to compose evaluation scenes. ComOb serves as a physically consistent simulation-based scene dataset, supporting both the training and evaluation of Tetris3D by supplying the necessary annotated environments for object interaction analysis.

assertion_evidence.description: The paper introduces ComOb as its simulation-based composited object scene dataset.
assertion_evidence.evidence: To address this, we introduce ComOb, a simulation-based physically consistent dataset of composite object scenes that captures physical interactions across diverse object categories, together with interaction-induced occlusions.

To address these limitations, we introduce ComOb, a large-scale simulation-based scene dataset in which general objects are arranged according to diverse interaction types, such as stacking and containment, and settled into physically stable configurations through physics simulation (Todorov et al., 2012).

These models, however, assume a clean image of a single object, whereas objects in real scenes occlude one another.

edges.description: TETRIS3D and DINOV3 represent a synergistic integration of advanced 3D reconstruction and vision foundation models. TETRIS3D leverages the DINOV3 feature map F to construct precise voxel-wise conditions, enabling robust 3D scene understanding. This process involves blending each DINOV3 patch feature with a learnable null embedding based on its occlusion ratio, effectively handling visibility and depth challenges. Together, these entities facilitate the creation of detailed 3D representations from 2D visual features, bridging the gap between image understanding and volumetric data generation.

edges.description: TETRIS3D is evaluated on the Toys4K dataset across multiple experiments, including quantitative comparisons in Tables 1, 4, and 5, qualitative results shown in Figure 4, and qualitative comparisons with baselines. The evaluation assesses reconstruction and physical stability metrics, where TETRIS3D retains the best performance among compared methods. One experiment specifically uses VLM-inferred relations, while another assesses sensitivity to depth estimation errors by replacing ground-truth depth maps from Stojanov et al. (2021) with predictions from MoGe3 (Kong et al., 2026), with all methods receiving the same estimated depth maps following the evaluation protocol. TETRIS3D reports results on Toys4K and is compared with baselines on the dataset.

edges.description: SAM-3D was evaluated on the Toys4K dataset (Stojanov et al., 2021) using estimated depth maps from MoGe3 (Kong et al., 2026) to assess sensitivity to depth estimation errors, with all methods receiving identical estimated depth maps following the evaluation protocol. According to Tab. 4, Tetris3D retained the best performance among compared methods across all reconstruction and physical stability metrics, showing lower penetration depth (PD) and mean displacement (Dmean), indicating less interpenetration and greater stability during simulation. Tetris3D also achieved the best MMD, COV, and P-FID scores. However, SAM-3D obtained higher Uni3D and ULIP scores than Tetris3D.

assertion_evidence.evidence: Table 4: Quantitative comparison on Toys4K (Stojanov et al., 2021) with estimated depth. We compare Tetris3D with baselines using depth maps estimated by MoGe3 (Kong et al., 2026). All methods requiring depth use the same depth maps.

assertion_evidence.description: Evaluation with Estimated Depth. To assess sensitivity to depth estimation errors, we replace the ground-truth depth maps used in the main Toys4K (Stojanov et al., 2021) comparison with predictions from MoGe3 (Kong et al., 2026). All methods receive the same estimated depth maps following our evaluation protocol. As shown in Tab. 4, Tetris3D retains the best performance among the compared methods across all reconstruction and physical stability metrics. In particular, its lower penetration depth (PD) and mean displacement (Dmean) indicate less interpenetration and greater stability during simulation. It also achieves the best MMD, COV, and P-FID, although SAM-3D obtains higher Uni3D and ULIP scores.

# W/O INTERACTION COND., P-FID, and POINT-E

The community consists of three entities: W/O INTERACTION COND., P-FID, and POINT-E. W/O INTERACTION COND. is an ablation configuration without interaction conditioning. P-FID is a generation quality metric that uses POINT-E, a point-cloud feature extractor released with the Point-E system. W/O INTERACTION COND. reports CD-S values, while P-FID uses POINT-E to measure generative quality.

## W/O INTERACTION COND. as an ablation configuration

W/O INTERACTION COND. is an ablation configuration without interaction conditioning. It reports CD-S values, which are likely used to evaluate the performance of the configuration. The entity has a degree of 15, indicating its significance within the community. [Data: Entities (161); Relationships (251)]

## P-FID as a generation quality metric

P-FID, or Perceptual Fréchet Inception Distance, is a generation quality metric used to measure generative quality. It calculates the Fréchet distance between the distributions of generated and ground-truth objects in the feature space of the point-cloud feature extractor released with Point-E. As a lower score indicates better performance, it is often denoted as P-FID ↓. This metric is reported in various tables, including Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5, to evaluate the quality of generated point clouds. P-FID uses POINT-E, a point-cloud feature extractor released alongside the Point-E system. [Data: Entities (117); Relationships (358)]

## POINT-E as a point-cloud feature extractor

POINT-E is a point-cloud feature extractor released alongside the Point-E system. It functions as a component designed to process and extract features from point cloud data, supporting the broader capabilities of the Point-E framework. POINT-E is used by P-FID to measure generative quality. [Data: Entities (291); Relationships (358)]

# W/ AMODAL3R ATTN and COV Metric Community

The community centers on the W/ AMODAL3R ATTN configuration, which utilizes an occlusion-aware attention module to improve visual understanding of occluded objects. This configuration reports the CD-S metric value and is linked to the COV generation quality metric through the SAM-3D system, which reports COV values. The relationships indicate a technical ecosystem focused on evaluating and enhancing generative model performance in visual tasks.

## W/ AMODAL3R ATTN configuration details

W/ AMODAL3R ATTN is a configuration that replaces V2I attention with the Amodal3R attention module. This configuration specifically utilizes the Amodal3R occlusion-aware attention module to handle occluded objects more effectively. By integrating this attention mechanism, the system enhances its ability to process visual information where objects may be partially hidden, improving overall performance in tasks requiring robust visual understanding. [Data: Entities (162)]

## Occlusion-aware attention module relationship

The W/ AMODAL3R ATTN configuration reports that it uses the occlusion-aware attention module from Amodal3R. This relationship highlights the specific technical component integrated into the configuration to address occlusion challenges in visual processing. [Data: Relationships (284)]

## CD-S metric reporting

The W/ AMODAL3R ATTN configuration reports the CD-S metric value. This indicates that the configuration is evaluated using the CD-S metric, which is part of the performance assessment for this visual understanding system. [Data: Relationships (269)]

## COV metric definition and usage

COV is a generation quality metric used to evaluate generative models against ground-truth object distributions. It measures coverage by calculating the fraction of ground-truth objects that are selected as the nearest neighbor of at least one generated object, with higher values indicating better performance. COV is defined in equation 14 and is reported as a metric in Table 1, Table 4, Tab. 4, and Table 5. It serves as both a coverage metric and a coverage generation quality metric, assessing how well generated objects cover the ground-truth distribution. [Data: Entities (116)]

## SAM-3D reporting COV metric

SAM-3D reports the COV metric value. This relationship shows that SAM-3D is a system that utilizes the COV metric for evaluating generative model performance, connecting it to the broader assessment framework within this community. [Data: Relationships (109)]

# GENA3D, SAM-3D, and OURS (VLM) 3D Generation Community

The community centers on 3D generation methods and evaluation metrics. GENA3D serves as an amodal generation baseline method marked with a dagger [Data: Entities (126)]. SAM-3D reports multiple metrics including IoU-B, MMD, UNI3D, and ULIP [Data: Relationships (106, 108, 111, 112)]. OURS (VLM) is a configuration of Tetris3D using VLM-inferred relations and reports CD-S [Data: Entities (295); Relationships (367)]. These entities are interconnected through shared metrics and datasets such as MessyKitchens and Picasso, forming a research community focused on bounding box reconstruction quality, generative quality, and semantic alignment of 3D point clouds.

## GENA3D as a baseline method

GENA3D is an amodal generation and pose estimation method marked with a dagger. It serves as an amodal generation baseline method and is identified as a baseline method marked with a dagger in Table 4 [Data: Entities (126)]. GENA3D reports CD-S on MessyKitchens and reports CD-S value [Data: Relationships (150)]. This positions GENA3D as a reference point within the community for evaluating other 3D generation approaches.

## SAM-3D's comprehensive metric reporting

SAM-3D reports the IoU-B metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets [Data: Relationships (106)]. SAM-3D reports MMD metric value [Data: Relationships (108)]. SAM-3D reports the Uni3D metric value and obtains higher Uni3D and ULIP scores compared to UNI3D [Data: Relationships (111)]. SAM-3D reports a ULIP metric value and achieves higher scores in both Uni3D and ULIP compared to another method [Data: Relationships (112)]. This demonstrates SAM-3D's central role in the community as a method evaluated across multiple quality dimensions.

## OURS (VLM) configuration and reporting

OURS (VLM) is a configuration of Tetris3D using VLM-inferred relations [Data: Entities (295)]. Ours (VLM) reports CD-S value [Data: Relationships (367)]. This entity represents a VLM-based approach within the community, contributing to the evaluation landscape through CD-S reporting.

## IoU-B as a reconstruction quality metric

IoU-B is a reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate the accuracy of bounding box reconstruction. It is calculated as the Intersection over Union for bounding boxes, measuring the overlap between predicted and ground-truth boxes [Data: Entities (113)]. This metric is commonly referenced in academic literature, specifically appearing in Table 1 and Table 5 [Data: Entities (113)]. It serves as a scene-level quality assessment tool where higher values indicate better reconstruction quality [Data: Entities (113)].

## MMD as a generative quality metric

MMD is a statistical metric used to measure the generative quality of models by comparing the distribution of generated data against the ground-truth object distribution [Data: Entities (115)]. Reported in units of 10⁻³, it serves as a critical quality metric across multiple tables (Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5) within the research [Data: Entities (115)]. A lower MMD value indicates a closer match between the generated and real data distributions [Data: Entities (115)]. This metric is formally defined in equation 14 and is also referenced as the Minimum Matching Distance [Data: Entities (115)].

## UNI3D and ULIP as semantic alignment metrics

UNI3D is a generation quality metric used to evaluate the semantic alignment between an input image and a generated point cloud [Data: Entities (118)]. It is reported as a performance score where higher values indicate better quality, denoted as Uni3D ↑ [Data: Entities (118)]. ULIP is a generation quality metric used to evaluate the semantic alignment between an input image and a generated point cloud [Data: Entities (119)]. It is reported as a score where higher values indicate better performance, denoted as ULIP ↑ [Data: Entities (119)]. Both metrics appear in Table 1 and Table 5 of the source material [Data: Entities (118, 119)].

reports.full_content:
# SAM-3D, SCENEMAKER, SCENEGEN, and Scene Reconstruction Metrics

The community centers on scene generation baseline methods SAM-3D, SCENEMAKER, and SCENEGEN and their evaluation using reconstruction quality and physical stability metrics CD-S, PD, and EPEAK. Relationships show that SAM-3D reports CD-S, PD, and EPEAK values on MessyKitchens and Picasso, while SCENEMAKER and SCENEGEN report CD-S values across these datasets. These entities are linked through performance reporting on shared datasets, indicating a cohesive evaluation framework for scene generation and reconstruction quality.

## SAM-3D as a central baseline method

SAM-3D is a method evaluated in Table 2 and listed in the Method column of Table 1. It serves as a baseline method in Table 4 and is compared as a method in Tab. 4. Additionally, SAM-3D is identified as a scene generation baseline method. [Data: Entities (106)] SAM-3D reports the CD-S metric value on MessyKitchens, providing CD-S values as part of its reporting functionality specifically for the MessyKitchens dataset. [Data: Relationships (102)] SAM-3D reports the PD metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. [Data: Relationships (113)] SAM-3D reports the EPEAK metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. [Data: Relationships (115)] These relationships position SAM-3D as a central entity connected to all three metrics and both datasets, highlighting its role in the evaluation framework.

## SCENEMAKER and SCENEGEN as scene generation baselines

SCENEMAKER is a scene generation baseline method listed in Table 2 under the Method column. [Data: Entities (131)] SCENEGEN is also a scene generation baseline method listed in Table 2 under the Method column. [Data: Entities (130)] SCENEMAKER and CD-S are associated with performance reporting on specific datasets. Reports indicate that the CD-S metric value was measured on MessyKitchens, and the CD-S metric value was also measured on Picasso. These findings document the application of the CD-S metric across both the MessyKitchens and Picasso environments within the SCENEMAKER context. [Data: Relationships (204)] SCENEGEN reports the CD-S metric on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. The CD-S metric is utilized by SCENEGEN to evaluate performance across these distinct datasets, providing a consistent measurement framework for assessing results on MessyKitchens and Picasso. [Data: Relationships (192)]

## CD-S as a scene-level reconstruction quality metric

CD-S is a reconstruction quality metric, specifically a scene-level Chamfer Distance for surface reconstruction quality. It measures the Chamfer distance at the scene level by concatenating the point sets of all objects within a scene. This metric is used to evaluate reconstruction quality, with lower values indicating better performance, as denoted by CD-S ↓. It is referenced as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5. [Data: Entities (109)] CD-S is reported by SAM-3D on MessyKitchens [Data: Relationships (102)], measured across MessyKitchens and Picasso in the SCENEMAKER context [Data: Relationships (204)], and reported by SCENEGEN on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (192)]. This demonstrates CD-S as a shared evaluation metric across multiple baseline methods and datasets.

## PD and EPEAK as physical stability metrics

PD, or Penetration Depth, is a physical stability metric used to quantify the extent of penetration or overlap between entities, calculated using the formula PD = 1/N ∑ᵢ₌₁ᴺ ∑ⱼ max{0, -ϕⱼ(xᵢ)}. This metric is referenced in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where lower values (PD ↓) indicate better physical stability. [Data: Entities (120)] EPEAK is a physical stability metric, also referred to as the Peak Energy metric or Peak error metric. It is included in Table 1 and measured in Table 5. The metric follows a downward trend, where lower EPEAK values indicate better physical stability (↓ Epeak ↓). [Data: Entities (122)] SAM-3D reports PD values on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (113)] and EPEAK values on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (115)], linking these physical stability metrics to the central baseline method.

## Shared datasets MessyKitchens and Picasso

The relationships indicate that SAM-3D reports CD-S on MessyKitchens [Data: Relationships (102)], PD on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (113)], and EPEAK on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (115)]. SCENEMAKER documents CD-S measurements on MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (204)]. SCENEGEN reports CD-S on both MessyKitchens and Picasso [Data: Relationships (192)]. The repeated use of MessyKitchens and Picasso across methods and metrics establishes these datasets as common evaluation environments within this community.

reports.full_content:
# WORLDSCULPT, SHAPER, MIDI, SAM-3D, and Reconstruction Metrics

The community centers on scene generation baseline methods WORLDSCULPT, SHAPER, and MIDI, alongside the SAM-3D method and several reconstruction quality and physical stability metrics. WORLDSCULPT reports CD-S on MessyKitchens, while SHAPER and MIDI also report CD-S on the same dataset. SAM-3D reports multiple metrics including CD-O, F1-S, F1-O, ICP-ROT, and DMEAN on MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets. These entities are interconnected through metric reporting relationships, forming a network of 3D reconstruction evaluation methods and quality indicators.

## WORLDSCULPT as a scene generation baseline method

WORLDSCULPT is a scene generation baseline method that extends Pixal3D to a multi-view setting for scene-level generation. It appears as a method entry in the Method column of Table 1 and Table 2, and is also identified as a baseline method in Table 4. WORLDSCULPT reports CD-S on MessyKitchens and reports CD-S value, establishing its role in the evaluation framework [Data: Entities (124); Relationships (132)].

## SHAPER as a compared baseline method

SHAPER is a baseline method included in Table 4 and is also compared in Table 1. It is listed in Table 2 and identified as a scene generation baseline method. SHAPER reports the CD-S metric on MessyKitchens and reports the CD-S value, showing its participation in the same evaluation context as WORLDSCULPT [Data: Entities (123); Relationships (117)].

## MIDI as a scene generation baseline method

MIDI is a method listed in Table 2 under the Method column and serves as a scene generation baseline method. MIDI reports CD-S on MessyKitchens, contributing to the set of baseline methods evaluated using the CD-S metric on this dataset [Data: Entities (129); Relationships (182)].

## SAM-3D as a multi-metric reporting method

SAM-3D reports the CD-O metric value, including its reporting on Picasso. SAM-3D reports the F1-S metric on the MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets. SAM-3D reports the F1-O metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. SAM-3D reports the ICP-ROT metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets. SAM-3D reports the DMEAN metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso, demonstrating its comprehensive metric coverage across multiple datasets [Data: Relationships (103, 104, 105, 107, 114)].

## CD-O as an object-level reconstruction quality metric

CD-O is a reconstruction quality metric that measures object-level Chamfer distance. It evaluates the geometric fidelity of individual object reconstructions by computing the Chamfer distance at the object level. CD-O is reported as a reconstruction quality metric in Table 1 and Table 5, with lower values indicating better performance (CD-O ↓). It is also referred to as Chamfer Distance for O, Chamfer Distance for Object reconstruction quality metric, Chamfer Distance for Objects metric, Chamfer distance for objects, and object-level Chamfer distance [Data: Entities (110); Relationships (103)].

## F1-S as a scene-level reconstruction quality metric

F1-S is a reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate surface reconstruction performance at the scene level. It is an F1 score for S, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This scene-level F1 score serves as a key indicator of reconstruction quality and is reported as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-S ↑ [Data: Entities (111); Relationships (104)].

## F1-O as an object-level reconstruction quality metric

F1-O is an object-level reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate the accuracy of reconstructed objects. It is an F1 score specifically for object reconstruction quality, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This metric appears in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-O ↑, indicating that higher values represent better reconstruction quality [Data: Entities (112); Relationships (105)].

## ICP-ROT as a rotation error metric

ICP-ROT is a reconstruction quality metric used to measure rotation error in 3D reconstruction processes. It is specifically designed to quantify the rotation component of the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm's performance. This metric is typically evaluated at the scene level and reported in tables such as Table 1 and Table 5, where lower values indicate better reconstruction quality [Data: Entities (114); Relationships (107)].

## DMEAN as a physical stability metric

DMEAN is a physical stability metric, also known as the Mean Distance metric, Mean Distance physical stability metric, Mean depth metric, Mean displacement metric, or Mean distance metric. It is a quantitative measure used to assess physical stability, with lower values indicating greater stability (Dmean ↓). DMEAN is documented as a metric in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5 [Data: Entities (121); Relationships (114)].

TETRIS3D sequentially generates objects autoregressively, conditioning each object on neighboring geometry and physical relations to achieve geometric and physical coherence. The framework is evaluated on synthetic datasets such as TOYS4K and real-world scene benchmarks, reporting superior performance across reconstruction, generation quality, and physical stability metrics. reports.full_content:
# TETRIS3D and 3D Scene Generation Framework

The community centers on TETRIS3D, a 3D scene generation framework built on TRELLIS.2 that reconstructs object-centric scenes from a single image. TETRIS3D sequentially generates objects autoregressively, conditioning each object on neighboring geometry and physical relations to achieve geometric and physical coherence. The framework is evaluated on synthetic datasets such as TOYS4K and real-world scene benchmarks, reporting superior performance across reconstruction, generation quality, and physical stability metrics. Key components include sparse structure generation, structured latent generation, visible-to-invisible attention, and VLM-based physical relation reasoning.

## TETRIS3D as the central framework

TETRIS3D is the central entity in this community, serving as a 3D scene generation framework introduced in the paper "TETRIS3D: 3D SCENE GENERATION WITH OBJECTS THAT FIT TOGETHER." It is built on TRELLIS.2 and functions as a generative framework for object-centric 3D scene reconstruction from a single image. The method sequentially generates objects autoregressively, explicitly conditioning each object on neighboring geometry and physical relations to achieve geometric and physical coherence among objects, even under occlusion. [Data: Entities (0); Relationships (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, +more)]

## Evaluation on TOYS4K and real-world benchmarks

TETRIS3D is evaluated on the TOYS4K dataset introduced by Stojanov et al. in 2021, which serves as a comprehensive evaluation resource used across multiple analyses in the associated research. The dataset is employed for both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, appearing in Table 1, Table 4, Table 5, Figure 4, and Figure 11. It is utilized in the main comparison and an ablation study, and is specifically used for evaluating VLM-inferred relations. TETRIS3D is also evaluated on real-world scene benchmarks with complex interactions and contacts, including those from Ansari et al. (2026) and Yu et al. (2026). [Data: Entities (108, 20, 21, 22); Relationships (101, 10, 11, 12, 243, +more)]

## Technical components and architecture

TETRIS3D includes several key technical components. It uses sparse structure generation and structured latent generation as its two-stage pipeline. The framework incorporates visible-to-invisible cross-attention layers for faithful completion of occluded parts. It uses per-token injection to derive conditions from depth maps, back-projected image features, and object interactions. TETRIS3D also uses image feature back-projection with depth maps to generate each object directly in the pose observed in the scene image. The framework represents spatial context using unsigned distance fields and uses direction vectors and surface normals as components of spatial context. [Data: Entities (230, 35, 93, 94, 159); Relationships (329, 25, 37, 29, 30, +more)]

## Vision-language model and physical relation reasoning

TETRIS3D uses a vision-language model (VLM) to infer a physical dependency hierarchy and derive generation order by topologically sorting this hierarchy. According to Bai et al. (2025), VLM infers relation types and a directed physical dependency hierarchy, establishing physical dependency order for autoregressive object generation. TETRIS3D uses VLM-based physical relation reasoning to determine physical relation types and establish physical dependency order among objects. The framework explicitly conditions generation on physical relations, using a predefined set of relation types encoded as learnable embeddings. [Data: Entities (17, 39, 77, 78, 156); Relationships (8, 28, 65, 66, 297, +more)]

## Performance metrics and reported results

TETRIS3D reports superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics. For scene-level quality, it reports scene-level chamfer distance (CD-S), F-score (F1-S), and residual rotation error after per-object ICP alignment (ICP-ROT). For object-level quality, it reports object-level chamfer distance (CD-O). For physical stability, it reports mean displacement (DMEAN) measuring settling error and penetration depth measured in initial configuration. TETRIS3D also reports cosine similarity for cross-modal consistency. The framework uses MMD and COV generative quality metrics from Achlioptas et al. (2018), P-FID generative quality metric from Nichol et al. (2022), ULIP semantic measure from Xue et al. (2024), and Uni3D semantic measure from Zhou et al. (2024). [Data: Entities (23, 24, 25, 135, 136, +more); Relationships (13, 14, 15, 227, 228, +more)]

## Training infrastructure and optimization

TETRIS3D uses AdamW optimizer for training and NVIDIA H200 GPUs as the hardware infrastructure. The framework employs classifier-free guidance using condition dropout. It uses a two-stage curriculum training strategy with Stage 1 and Stage 2. During training, TETRIS3D uses depth augmentation, observed depth points, and Gaussian noise to perturb observed depth points. The framework also uses SAM3 for object mask extraction and QWEN3-VL-30B to extract distinct object instances. [Data: Entities (226, 227, 229, 241, 242, +more); Relationships (313, 314, 315, 324, 325, +more)]

## Comparison with related methods and baselines

TETRIS3D is compared with agentic generation tool GPT-6 ASTRA from OpenAI. The framework follows the protocol of Axolotl3D for synthetic occlusion. TETRIS3D reports results on large-scale 3D datasets from Deitke et al. (2023B;A) and encodes shapes as unordered sets of latent vectors following Zhang et al. (2023; 2024), Li et al. (2025), and Zhao et al. (2025B). The framework also reports on attaching latents to sparse voxel grids following Xiang et al. (2025; 2026) and Wu et al. (2026), and on completing occluded objects in 3D latent space following Wu et al. (2025), Hu & Shugrina (2026), and Zhou & Tai (2025). [Data: Entities (132, 237, 169, 170, 171, +more); Relationships (218, 323, 291, 292, 293, +more)]}],

reports.full_content:
# TETRIS3D and Object Interaction-Aware Generation

The community centers on TETRIS3D, a generation process that explicitly conditions on spatial context to incorporate object interactions. Key entities include SPATIAL CONTEXT, OBJECT INTERACTION-AWARE GENERATION, OBJECT-INTERACTION CONDITION, PER-VOXEL INTERACTION CONDITION, and RELATION TYPE. These entities are linked through relationships describing how TETRIS3D uses spatial context, how object interaction-aware generation uses spatial context and per-voxel interaction conditions, and how object-interaction conditions include spatial context and relation types.

## TETRIS3D conditions generation on spatial context

TETRIS3D explicitly conditions its generation process on spatial context, incorporating object interactions into the generation process. This approach allows TETRIS3D to leverage spatial relationships and contextual information to produce more coherent and contextually appropriate outputs. By integrating spatial context directly into its generation framework, TETRIS3D ensures that the resulting content reflects the intended spatial arrangements and interactions between objects. [Data: Relationships (31); Entities (42)]

## Object interaction-aware generation uses spatial context

The object interaction-aware generation component is a method section describing object interaction-aware generation. This component focuses on generating content that is aware of interactions between objects, ensuring that the generated outputs accurately reflect how objects relate to and affect one another. By incorporating object interaction awareness, the generation process produces more coherent, contextually appropriate, and realistic results. The method section outlines the specific techniques and approaches used to achieve this object interaction-aware generation, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding how object relationships are modeled and integrated into the generation process. [Data: Entities (68); Relationships (67)]

## Object-interaction condition includes spatial context and relation type

The object-interaction condition is a condition incorporating spatial context and relation type. It includes spatial context as a component and also includes relation type as a component. # COMOB Dataset and Its Supporting Components

The community centers on COMOB, a large-scale simulation-based dataset for physically consistent scenes. COMOB relies on a PHYSICS ENGINE to settle target objects into stable configurations and uses PHYSICS SIMULATION for object placement. It also sources target objects from TRELLIS-500K, which contains approximately 400,000 unique objects used to construct scenes. These relationships indicate a tightly integrated technical pipeline for generating and studying physical interactions in composite object scenes.

## COMOB as a large-scale simulation dataset

COMOB is a large-scale, simulation-based dataset designed to provide physically consistent scenes with explicit object interaction annotations. It features 1.2 million scenes showcasing diverse object categories in physically stable configurations. The dataset includes per-object meshes, target-object images, normal maps, training viewpoints, and pairwise physical relation annotations. Additionally, it captures interaction-induced occlusions across various interaction types. Described in Section 3.4, COMOB is used for training and serves as a comprehensive resource for studying physical interactions in composite object scenes. [Data: Entities (2)]

## COMOB's use of a physics engine

COMOB uses a physics engine to settle target objects into physically stable configurations, ensuring that simulated objects behave according to realistic physical laws. The PHYSICS ENGINE is a tool designed for simulating physical stability. This relationship is critical because it underpins the physical consistency of the scenes generated by COMOB. [Data: Entities (2, 105); Relationships (100)]

## COMOB's reliance on physics simulation

COMOB uses physics simulation to settle objects into physically stable configurations. PHYSICS SIMULATION is used to settle objects into physically stable configurations. This relationship reinforces the physical realism of the dataset and supports the generation of stable object arrangements within scenes. [Data: Entities (2, 18); Relationships (16)]

## COMOB's use of TRELLIS-500K target objects

The ComOb dataset is constructed using target objects sourced from TRELLIS-500K, and it utilizes these same target objects from TRELLIS-500K for its composition. TRELLIS-500K is a dataset containing approximately 400,000 unique target objects used to generate scenes. It serves as a source of target objects used to construct scenes. This relationship indicates that COMOB depends on TRELLIS-500K as a foundational object library for scene composition. [Data: Entities (2, 104); Relationships (99)]

## Technical pipeline for physical interaction research

The community forms a technical pipeline where TRELLIS-500K provides target objects, the PHYSICS ENGINE and PHYSICS SIMULATION ensure physical stability, and COMOB integrates these components to produce 1.2 million physically consistent scenes with interaction annotations. This integrated structure makes COMOB a comprehensive resource for studying physical interactions in composite object scenes, with potential applications in training and simulation research. reports.full_content:
# SAM-3D, TETRIS3D, and 3D Generation Metrics Community

This community centers on 3D generation and reconstruction research, with SAM-3D and TETRIS3D as key model entities. SAM-3D reports multiple quality metrics including IoU-B, MMD, COV, UNI3D, ULIP, and P-FID, while TETRIS3D serves as the base configuration for W/ AMODAL3R ATTN and W/O INTERACTION COND. The community includes evaluation datasets such as Toys4K, MessyKitchens, and Picasso, along with supporting components like Point-E and FoundationPose. These entities are interconnected through reporting, construction, evaluation, and usage relationships, forming a research ecosystem focused on 3D point cloud generation quality assessment.

## SAM-3D reports multiple 3D generation quality metrics

SAM-3D is a central entity in this community, reporting several key 3D generation quality metrics. It reports the IoU-B metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets, serving as a scene-level quality assessment tool where higher values indicate better reconstruction quality [Data: Relationships (106); Entities (113)]. SAM-3D also reports MMD, a statistical metric measuring generative quality by comparing generated data distribution against ground-truth object distribution, reported in units of 10⁻³ across Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5 [Data: Relationships (108); Entities (115)]. Additionally, SAM-3D reports COV, which measures coverage by calculating the fraction of ground-truth objects selected as the nearest neighbor of at least one generated object, with higher values indicating better performance [Data: Relationships (109); Entities (116)]. These reporting relationships establish SAM-3D as a comprehensive evaluation subject across multiple quality dimensions.

## SAM-3D demonstrates competitive performance in Uni3D and ULIP metrics

SAM-3D is evaluated using multiple 3D generation metrics alongside UNI3D and ULIP. SAM-3D reports the Uni3D metric value and obtains higher Uni3D and ULIP scores compared to UNI3D, where higher values indicate better quality for semantic alignment between input images and generated point clouds [Data: Relationships (111); Entities (118)]. Similarly, SAM-3D reports a ULIP metric value and achieves higher scores in both Uni3D and ULIP compared to another method [Data: Relationships (112); Entities (119)]. However, UNI3D achieves the best performance in MMD, COV, and P-FID metrics, indicating that each model excels in different aspects of 3D generation quality [Data: Relationships (111); Entities (115, 116, 117)]. This competitive landscape suggests that SAM-3D leads in semantic alignment metrics while other methods lead in distribution matching and coverage metrics.

## P-FID relies on Point-E feature extractor for perceptual distance measurement

P-FID, or Perceptual Fréchet Inception Distance, is a generation quality metric that measures generative quality by calculating the Fréchet distance between distributions of generated and ground-truth objects in the feature space of the point-cloud feature extractor released with Point-E [Data: Entities (117)]. P-FID uses the point-cloud feature extractor released with Point-E, establishing a dependency relationship where P-FID relies on Point-E's component for processing and extracting features from point cloud data [Data: Relationships (358); Entities (291)]. As a lower P-FID score indicates better performance, this metric is reported in various tables including Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5 to evaluate the quality of generated point clouds [Data: Entities (117)]. This relationship highlights the importance of feature extraction components in perceptual quality assessment.

## TETRIS3D serves as base for ablation and attention configurations

TETRIS3D functions as a foundational configuration in this community, with W/ AMODAL3R ATTN constructed from TETRIS3D as a configuration that replaces V2I attention with the Amodal3R attention module [Data: Relationships (250); Entities (162)]. This configuration specifically utilizes the Amodal3R occlusion-aware attention module to handle occluded objects more effectively, enhancing the system's ability to process visual information where objects may be partially hidden [Data: Entities (162)]. Additionally, W/O INTERACTION COND. is an ablation configuration derived from TETRIS3D, representing a configuration without interaction conditioning [Data: Relationships (249); Entities (161)]. These construction relationships demonstrate TETRIS3D's role as a base model from which specialized variants are derived for different architectural experiments.

## Ours (VLM) configuration evaluated on Toys4K dataset

OURS (VLM) is a configuration of Tetris3D using VLM-inferred relations that has been evaluated on the Toys4K dataset [Data: Relationships (366); Entities (295)]. This evaluation relationship indicates that the VLM-inferred relations configuration undergoes empirical testing on the Toys4K dataset, which likely contains 3D object data for assessing generation performance. The combined degree of 26 for this relationship suggests significant connectivity within the community, indicating that this evaluation is an important aspect of the research ecosystem. This finding shows that the community includes not only metric reporting and model construction but also dataset-specific evaluation of novel configurations.

## GENA3D requires FoundationPose for scene alignment and placement

GENA3D is an amodal generation and pose estimation method marked with a dagger, serving as an amodal generation baseline method identified in Table 4 [Data: Entities (126)]. GENA3D results require alignment using FoundationPose, and GENA3D is paired with FoundationPose for placement in the scene [Data: Relationships (148); Entities (148)]. This usage relationship establishes that GENA3D depends on FoundationPose for proper alignment and placement within 3D scenes, highlighting the interdependence between generation methods and pose estimation components. The combined degree of 21 for this relationship indicates substantial connectivity, suggesting that FoundationPose plays a significant role in the community's methodological framework.

## Community encompasses multiple evaluation datasets and metric tables

The research community spans multiple evaluation datasets including MessyKitchens, Picasso, and Toys4K, with metrics reported across Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5 [Data: Relationships (106, 108, 109, 111, 112); Entities (113, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]. IoU-B appears in Table 1 and Table 5, MMD appears in Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5, COV appears in Table 1, Table 4, Tab. 4, and Table 5, UNI3D appears in Table 1 and Table 5, ULIP appears in Table 1 and Table 5, and P-FID appears in Table 1, Table 4, and Table 5 [Data: Entities (113, 115, 116, 118, 119, 117)]. This widespread reporting across multiple tables and datasets indicates a comprehensive evaluation framework where different metrics assess different aspects of 3D generation quality, from bounding box reconstruction to semantic alignment and distributional similarity.

# SAM-3D, WorldSculpt, Shaper, and Scene Generation Baselines

The community centers on scene generation baseline methods and reconstruction quality metrics. SAM-3D is the most connected entity, reporting multiple metrics on MessyKitchens and Picasso. WorldSculpt and Shaper are evaluated on Toys4K, while SceneMaker is evaluated on MessyKitchens. Metrics such as CD-S, CD-O, F1-S, F1-O, ICP-ROT, PD, DMEAN, and EPEAK are used to assess reconstruction quality and physical stability across these datasets.

## SAM-3D as a central baseline method

SAM-3D is a scene generation baseline method evaluated in Table 2 and listed in the Method column of Table 1. It serves as a baseline method in Table 4 and is compared as a method in Tab. 4. SAM-3D reports the CD-S metric value on MessyKitchens, CD-O metric value including its reporting on Picasso, F1-S metric on MessyKitchens and Picasso, F1-O metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso, ICP-ROT metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso datasets, PD metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso, DMEAN metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso, and EPEAK metric value on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (102, 103, 104, 105, 107, 113, 114, 115)]

## WorldSculpt and Shaper evaluated on Toys4K

WorldSculpt is a scene generation baseline method that extends Pixal3D to a multi-view setting for scene-level generation. It appears as a method entry in the Method column of Table 1 and Table 2, and is also identified as a baseline method in Table 4. WorldSculpt was evaluated on Toys4K, specifically on the Toys4K dataset. Shaper is a baseline method included in Table 4 and is also compared in Table 1. It is listed in Table 2 and identified as a scene generation baseline method. ShapeR evaluated on Toys4K dataset. [Data: Entities (124, 123); Relationships (131, 116)]

## SceneMaker evaluated on MessyKitchens

SceneMaker is a scene generation baseline method listed in Table 2 under the Method column. It is evaluated on MessyKitchens dataset. [Data: Entities (131); Relationships (202)]

## Reconstruction quality metrics used across methods

CD-S is a reconstruction quality metric, specifically a scene-level Chamfer Distance for surface reconstruction quality. It measures the Chamfer distance at the scene level by concatenating the point sets of all objects within a scene. This metric is used to evaluate reconstruction quality, with lower values indicating better performance, as denoted by CD-S ↓. It is referenced as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5. CD-O is a reconstruction quality metric that measures object-level Chamfer distance. It evaluates the geometric fidelity of individual object reconstructions by computing the Chamfer distance at the object level. CD-O is reported as a reconstruction quality metric in Table 1 and Table 5, with lower values indicating better performance (CD-O ↓). F1-S is a reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate surface reconstruction performance at the scene level. It is an F1 score for S, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This scene-level F1 score serves as a key indicator of reconstruction quality and is reported as a metric in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-S ↑. F1-O is an object-level reconstruction quality metric used to evaluate the accuracy of reconstructed objects. It is an F1 score specifically for object reconstruction quality, combining precision and recall derived by thresholding nearest-neighbour distances at τ. This metric appears in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5, where it is denoted as F1-O ↑, indicating that higher values represent better reconstruction quality. [Data: Entities (109, 110, 111, 112); Relationships (102, 103, 104, 105, 182, 192)]

## Physical stability metrics used across methods

ICP-ROT is a reconstruction quality metric used to measure rotation error in 3D reconstruction processes. It is specifically designed to quantify the rotation component of the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm's performance. This metric is typically evaluated at the scene level and reported in tables such as Table 1 and Table 5, where lower values indicate better reconstruction quality. PD, or Penetration Depth, is a physical stability metric used to quantify the extent of penetration or overlap between entities, calculated using the formula PD = 1/N ∑ᵢ₌₁ᴺ ∑ⱼ max{0, -ϕⱼ(xᵢ)}. This metric is referenced in Table 1 and measured in Table 5, where lower values (PD ↓) indicate better physical stability. DMEAN is a physical stability metric, also known as the Mean Distance metric, Mean Distance physical stability metric, Mean depth metric, Mean displacement metric, or Mean distance metric. It is a quantitative measure used to assess physical stability, with lower values indicating greater stability (Dmean ↓). DMEAN is documented as a metric in Table 1 and is measured in Table 5. EPEAK is a physical stability metric, also referred to as the Peak Energy metric or Peak error metric. It is included in Table 1 and measured in Table 5. The metric follows a downward trend, where lower EPEAK values indicate better physical stability (↓ Epeak ↓). [Data: Entities (114, 120, 121, 122); Relationships (107, 113, 114, 115)]

## MIDI and SceneGen as additional baseline methods

MIDI is a method listed in Table 2 under the Method column and serves as a scene generation baseline method. MIDI reports CD-S on MessyKitchens. SceneGen is a scene generation baseline method listed in Table 2 under the Method column. SCENEGEN reports the CD-S metric on both MessyKitchens and Picasso. The CD-S metric is utilized by SCENEGEN to evaluate performance across these distinct datasets, providing a consistent measurement framework for assessing results on MessyKitchens and Picasso. [Data: Entities (129, 130); Relationships (182, 192)]}],

# Optimal Topological Sort and Physical Dependency Hierarchy

The community centers on the Optimal Topological Sort algorithm, which computes generation order from physical dependency edges. The algorithm uses multiple inputs including Plane, Color Instance-Segmentation Image, Object Inventory JSON, Original RGB Scene Image, Physical Dependency Hierarchy, Confidence, In-Degree, PossiblePredecessors, StartState, FullState, DeletionCost, NextState, Parent, Cost, RGB, and JSON. These entities form a tightly coupled computational pipeline for physical dependency reasoning.

## Optimal Topological Sort as central algorithm

Optimal Topological Sort is the primary entity in this community, serving as the algorithm for computing generation order from physical dependency edges. It has a degree of 21, indicating it is highly connected within the network. The algorithm uses Plane as its root node and operates on the physical dependency hierarchy to determine processing order. [Data: Entities (309); Relationships (395, 400, 401, 402, 403, +more)]

## Input data entities supporting the algorithm

The algorithm relies on several input data entities including Color Instance-Segmentation Image, Object Inventory JSON, Original RGB Scene Image, and Physical Dependency Hierarchy. These entities provide the visual and structural information needed for physical dependency reasoning. The Color Instance-Segmentation Image contains objects painted in unique flat RGB colors, while the Object Inventory JSON provides descriptions and instance RGB colors for each object. [Data: Entities (311, 312, 313, 314); Relationships (400, 401, 402, 403)]

## Graph properties and state management

The algorithm utilizes graph properties such as In-Degree to identify the root node and PossiblePredecessors for each vertex. It manages state through StartState containing only Plane, FullState containing all objects, NextState formed by adding a vertex, and records Parent for each state. Cost and DeletionCost are maintained for each state during processing. [Data: Entities (317, 318, 319, 320, 321, 322, 323, 324); Relationships (405, 406, 407, 408, 409, 410, 411, 412)]

## Color and format specifications

RGB color format is used in instance segmentation and object inventory, while JSON format is used for object inventory entries. These format specifications ensure consistent data representation throughout the algorithm's processing pipeline. The Confidence level is associated with physical dependency edges and used for edge deletion decisions. [Data: Entities (316, 325, 326); Relationships (404, 413, 414)]

## Community impact and technical significance

This community represents a specialized computational framework for physical dependency reasoning in scene understanding. The tight coupling between the algorithm and its supporting entities suggests a well-defined technical system with clear data flow and processing stages. The impact is primarily technical rather than social or legal, focusing on algorithmic efficiency and accuracy in physical dependency analysis. [Data: Entities (309, 314); Relationships (395, 403, 409)]}],

# Interaction-Specific Placement and Predefined Interaction Types

The community centers on Interaction-Specific Placement, a method for generating scenes with predefined interactions. It is directly related to five interaction types: STACK, LEAN, CONTAIN, TOUCH, and PILE. Interaction-Specific Placement uses each of these interaction types, forming a structured framework for physical object relations in scene generation.

## Interaction-Specific Placement as the central method

Interaction-Specific Placement is the central entity in this community, described as a method for generating scenes with predefined interactions. It has a degree of 6, indicating it is highly connected within the network. This entity serves as the primary framework that organizes and utilizes the various predefined interaction types. [Data: Entities (261); Relationships (338, 339, 340, 342, 341)]

## STACK interaction type

STACK is a predefined interaction type characterized by a directed physical relation in which object A relies on object B for support. In this configuration, object A is positioned atop object B, depending on B to bear its weight and maintain stability. The relationship is directional, meaning the support flows from B to A. Interaction-Specific Placement uses the stack interaction, as indicated by the relationship between these entities. [Data: Entities (262); Relationships (338)]

## LEAN interaction type

LEAN is a directed physical relation where object A relies on object B for support, and it is classified as a predefined interaction type. This interaction type is used by Interaction-Specific Placement, contributing to the method's ability to generate scenes with varied physical dependencies between objects. [Data: Entities (263); Relationships (339)]

## CONTAIN interaction type

CONTAIN is a predefined interaction type characterized by a directed physical relation where object A relies on object B for support. This relationship establishes a dependency in which one object is supported or held by another within a structured interaction framework. Interaction-Specific Placement uses the contain interaction to model such dependencies in scene generation. [Data: Entities (264); Relationships (340)]

## TOUCH interaction type

TOUCH is a predefined interaction type characterized as an undirected physical contact relation that does not involve load-bearing support. Unlike STACK, LEAN, and CONTAIN, TOUCH does not imply a directional support dependency. Interaction-Specific Placement uses the touch interaction to represent simple physical contact between objects. [Data: Entities (266); Relationships (342)]

## PILE interaction type

PILE is described as a predefined interaction type. Interaction-Specific Placement uses the pile interaction, completing the set of five interaction types utilized by the method. PILE has a degree of 1, suggesting it is less connected than the other interaction types in this community. [Data: Entities (265); Relationships (341)]

reports.full_content:
# Object Grid G and Conditioning Framework

The community centers on Object Grid G, a spatial framework for voxels associated with pose-aligned generation. It serves as the foundation for image, depth, and general conditions (CIMG, CDEPTH, CINT), which are constructed from it. The grid also forms the Invisible Token Set, which is used by the Cross-Attention Layer alongside the Visible Token Set, and is defined by the Occlusion Mask. These relationships indicate a tightly integrated technical system for conditional generation.

## Object Grid G as the central spatial framework

Object Grid G is a schematic grid described in Section 3.2.1, corresponding to voxels, and serves as the spatial framework on which cimg, cdepth, and cint are defined. It is associated with pose-aligned generation and has a degree of 6, indicating its centrality in the community [Data: Entities (59)]. The grid is the target of multiple construction relationships from CIMG, CDEPTH, and CINT, confirming its role as the underlying structure for these conditions [Data: Relationships (81, 82, 83)]. Additionally, Object Grid G has a component relationship with the Invisible Token Set, where its tokens form that set [Data: Relationships (95)]. This central position suggests that changes to Object Grid G would propagate across the conditioning framework.

## Conditions constructed from Object Grid G

CIMG, CDEPTH, and CINT are all conditions defined on Object Grid G. CIMG is the image condition, CDEPTH is the depth condition, and CINT is a general condition, each with a degree of 1 [Data: Entities (89, 90, 91)]. Each is constructed from Object Grid G, as indicated by relationships with combined degrees of 7 [Data: Relationships (81, 82, 83)]. This construction relationship implies that these conditions inherit the spatial properties of the grid and are tightly coupled to its definition. Their low individual degrees suggest they are specialized components dependent on the central grid rather than independent entities.

## Invisible Token Set derived from Object Grid G

The Invisible Token Set consists of tokens whose voxels lie along camera rays through occlusion pixels, with a degree of 3 [Data: Entities (99)]. Object Grid G has a component relationship with this set, where object grid G tokens form the invisible token set, with a combined degree of 9 [Data: Relationships (95)]. This high combined degree indicates a strong association between the grid and the token set. The Occlusion Mask also uses the Invisible Token Set, defining it based on pixels occupied by other objects as potential occlusions of the target [Data: Entities (98); Relationships (97)]. This relationship suggests that the invisible tokens are specifically tied to occlusion reasoning within the system.

## Cross-Attention Layer utilizes both token sets

The Cross-Attention Layer is an additional layer with invisible tokens as queries and visible tokens as keys and values, with a degree of 3 [Data: Entities (101)]. It uses the Invisible Token Set as queries in a relationship with a combined degree of 6 [Data: Relationships (93)]. It also uses the Visible Token Set as keys and values in a relationship with a combined degree of 5 [Data: Relationships (94)]. The Visible Token Set comprises all remaining tokens not in the invisible token set and has a degree of 2 [Data: Entities (100)]. This dual usage indicates that the cross-attention mechanism integrates both occluded and non-occluded token information, likely enabling the model to reason about visible and hidden regions simultaneously.

## Occlusion Mask defines invisible tokens through occlusion reasoning

The Occlusion Mask treats all pixels occupied by other objects as potential occlusions of the target and has a degree of 1 [Data: Entities (98)]. It uses the Invisible Token Set in a relationship with a combined degree of 4 [Data: Relationships (97)]. This relationship indicates that the mask plays a role in determining which tokens are classified as invisible based on occlusion geometry. By linking the mask to the invisible token set, the system connects pixel-level occlusion reasoning with token-level representations used in cross-attention.

# Sparse Structure and Diffusion Model Components

The community centers on sparse structural representations and diffusion model components designed for structured latent generation. Key entities include SPARSE STRUCTURE (SS), VSS Θ, VSLAT Θ, VISIBLE-TO-INVISIBLE (V2I) CROSS-ATTENTION, and VISIBLE TOKENS. These entities are interconnected through generative and attentional relationships, where SS and VSS Θ serve as foundational structure generators, VSLAT Θ and V2I CROSS-ATTENTION refine latent representations, and VISIBLE TOKENS act as information sources for occluded region completion. The relationships indicate a pipeline from sparse structure generation to structured latent processing and cross-attention mechanisms.

## SPARSE STRUCTURE (SS) as the foundational binary occupancy grid

SPARSE STRUCTURE (SS) is a binary occupancy grid outlining coarse geometry with a degree of 2, serving as a foundational entity in the community. It is the target of TRELLIS.2, which generates the sparse structure, and the source for VSS Θ, which denoises a dense latent volume derived from SS. This positioning establishes SS as the primary geometric scaffold upon which other diffusion components operate. [Data: Entities (29), Relationships (17, 23)]

## VSS Θ and VSLAT Θ as complementary DiT model components

VSS Θ and VSLAT Θ are both Diffusion Transformer (DiT) layer components designed for structured generation, operating at different stages of the latent processing pipeline. VSS Θ functions as the first DiT to denoise a dense latent volume on a coarse grid, while VSLAT Θ serves as a second DiT specifically designed to process only active voxels for efficient structured latent generation. Their complementary roles suggest a two-stage denoising and generation process for structured data. [Data: Entities (33, 34), Relationships (24)]

## VISIBLE-TO-INVISIBLE (V2I) CROSS-ATTENTION mechanism for occluded region completion

VISIBLE-TO-INVISIBLE (V2I) CROSS-ATTENTION is an explicit mechanism with a degree of 5 that updates occluded parts by aggregating information from visible tokens. It guides the completion of hidden areas, functioning as a critical attentional bridge between visible and occluded data regions. This mechanism is directly utilized by the relationship between VISIBLE TOKENS and itself, highlighting its role in reconstructing missing geometric or semantic information. [Data: Entities (38), Relationships (32)]

## VISIBLE TOKENS as the information source for completion processes

VISIBLE TOKENS are entities with a degree of 1 that serve as the aggregated information source guiding the completion of occluded regions. They are the target of V2I CROSS-ATTENTION, which uses information aggregated from these visible tokens to inform the reconstruction of hidden areas. This establishes VISIBLE TOKENS as the primary data source for any inpainting or completion process within the community. [Data: Entities (49), Relationships (32)]

## Interconnected generative pipeline from structure to attention

The entities within this community form a connected generative pipeline starting with SPARSE STRUCTURE (SS), progressing through VSS Θ denoising, and potentially integrating VSLAT Θ for structured latent generation. The pipeline culminates with VISIBLE-TO-INVISIBLE (V2I) CROSS-ATTENTION and VISIBLE TOKENS for occluded region completion, demonstrating a comprehensive workflow from coarse geometry generation to detailed latent refinement and reconstruction. [Data: Relationships (17, 23, 24, 32)]

reports.full_content:
# TRELLIS.2 and DINOV3 3D Shape Generation Community

The community centers on TRELLIS.2, a 3D shape generation framework that utilizes a two-stage pipeline with a 30-block DiT backbone for each stage. TRELLIS.2 is related to DINOV3, a frozen image encoder providing patch features, and employs flow-matching formulation and diffusion transformer architecture for each stage. The framework also includes a sparse structure component and image condition masking technique that blends DINOv3 patch features with a learnable null embedding based on occlusion ratio.

## TRELLIS.2 as the central 3D shape generation framework

TRELLIS.2 serves as the central entity in this community, functioning as a 3D shape generation framework that utilizes a two-stage pipeline. Its base model consists of a 30-block DiT backbone for each generation stage, establishing it as a sophisticated technical system. The framework additionally employs a voxel-based generative backbone, which is also used by TETRIS3D, indicating shared architectural approaches within the broader 3D generation domain. [Data: Entities (16); Relationships (17, 20, 21, 22)]

## DINOV3 as a critical feature encoding component

DINOV3 is a frozen image encoder that provides patch features and input image features, and is also used as a feature map tool to construct voxel-wise conditions. This component plays a crucial role in the TRELLIS.2 pipeline by supplying the visual features that condition the generation process. The relationship between TRELLIS.2 and DINOV3 indicates that both stages of the framework are conditioned on input image features from this frozen encoder, making it a foundational dependency for the system's operation. [Data: Entities (26); Relationships (22, 307)]

## Flow-matching formulation as the modeling approach

The flow-matching formulation is used to model each stage of the TRELLIS.2 framework. This mathematical approach underpins the generative process, providing the theoretical basis for how the system transforms noise into structured 3D outputs. The use of flow-matching across both stages suggests a consistent modeling strategy throughout the pipeline, which may contribute to the framework's coherence and effectiveness in 3D shape generation. [Data: Entities (27); Relationships (20)]

## Diffusion transformer architecture as the model backbone

The diffusion transformer (DiT) serves as the model architecture for each stage of the TRELLIS.2 framework. With a 30-block DiT backbone for each generation stage, this architecture represents a significant computational investment and technical sophistication. The diffusion transformer approach combines the strengths of diffusion models with transformer attention mechanisms, enabling the framework to handle complex 3D shape generation tasks with high fidelity. [Data: Entities (28); Relationships (21)]

## Sparse structure as a key framework component

TRELLIS.2 first generates the sparse structure as a component of its two-stage pipeline. This sparse structure generation represents an initial phase in the framework's output production, likely establishing the basic geometric form before refinement in subsequent stages. The sparse structure component is integral to the framework's overall architecture and contributes to its ability to generate detailed 3D shapes efficiently. [Data: Entities (16); Relationships (17)]

## Image condition masking technique for feature blending

Image condition masking is a technique that blends DINOv3 patch features with a learnable null embedding based on occlusion ratio. This technique allows the framework to handle partially occluded or incomplete input images by adaptively weighting the visual features against a learned null embedding. The relationship between image condition masking and DINOV3 shows that this technique directly processes DINOv3 patch features, integrating them into the generation pipeline with occlusion-aware conditioning. [Data: Entities (219); Relationships (307)]}]}</think>{
